projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Robert Noyer was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Harold Phillips
sp.p: Oral history interview of World War II veterans conducted by Harold Phillips for the Handley Library archives and the Winchester-Frederick County Historical Society. Today is the 12th of February 2002. The veteran is Mr. Robert Noyer.

sp.speaker: Robert Noyer
sp.p: My name is Robert O. Noyer, N-O-Y-E-R. I was born 8/31/23 in Kearney, Nebraska. That's K-E-A-R-N-E-Y, Kearney, Nebraska.

sp.speaker: Harold Phillips
sp.p: Where did you go to school?

sp.speaker: Robert Noyer
sp.p: Which school?

sp.speaker: Harold Phillips
sp.p: Yeah. Which school?

sp.speaker: Robert Noyer
sp.p: Grade school? High school?

sp.speaker: Harold Phillips
sp.p: High school.

sp.speaker: Robert Noyer
sp.p: College?

sp.speaker: Harold Phillips
sp.p: College, yes.

sp.speaker: Robert Noyer
sp.p: I graduated in 1949 with a degree of electrical engineer from Purdue University.

sp.speaker: Harold Phillips
sp.p: Oh, I went to Purdue.

sp.speaker: Robert Noyer
sp.p: Prior to that, I graduated from high school in 1941 from a laboratory school connected with Ball State Teachers College in Muncie, Indiana. I graduated in June of '41.

sp.speaker: Harold Phillips
sp.p: Where were you Pearl Harbor Day?

sp.speaker: Robert Noyer
sp.p: Pearl Harbor Day, I was in Muncie, Indiana, building a ham radio transmitter. I remember it quite well. I was -- We left Nebraska in 1927, moving to Indiana, where my father was to be dean of the college at Ball State -- Ball State Teachers College. It's now Ball State University. I attended Ball State for a year from '41 until June of '42. And I was -- my was father was head of my draft board, which made things a little tense around town, because other people were being drafted, and I wasn't, even though I was in school. So that summer, I did not go to summer school, as I had planned, and I took a course in arc welding at a vocational school in town. And that was a choice of either go to that school or go to work on one of the two family farms in Northern Virginia -- in Northern Indiana, that I had to work on ever since I was about 10, and I didn't like that very much. So I went to welding school. I thought it would be cooler. It turned out it was exceedingly hot. In the fall of '42, the draft situation was getting difficult, not that my number was coming up, but there was a lot of talk in town about how the head of the draft board's eligible son was still running around loose. And so I didn't start back in school, but I took a job as a welder in the shipyards in and around Chicago -- they were making destroyer escorts -- welded there for a while. And in December my chance to enlist came along. My mother didn't want me to go in, but she was busy away in another town, helping her brother who had a terminal illness. So while she was away, my father and I went to the basement of the post office in Muncie, Indiana, and I raised my right hand and enlisted in the Navy in the aviation cadet program called "V-5." There's V-5. V-1 was a mid shipment, thing, I guess, for ships, and there was V-12, which was some sort of an academic thing. But I wanted to fly, and I had been flying prior to that, and I had some flight experience. In fact, I had actually soloed before then. So I awaited my call to go to flight school, and while I was waiting, I just kept on working. I made a good bit of money. In fact, I was making a dollar thirty-five an hour, which was large wages in those days, along with war the bonds, which are usually ___. I got my orders for active duty in June of 1943, with the war about half over. So I went into training, and I was sent to Greencastle, Indiana, to an academic course called "flight prep." And I think the problem was with the Navy, they were getting too many naval aviators, and they were lengthening out the training requirements as long as they could. So I went down there for about two months, and then I was transferred, paradoxically, back to my hometown of Muncie, Indiana, where I went to a flight school, where I actually learned to solo before, sent to this flight school. The term was WTS, War Training Service, and we learned to fly the ubiquitous Piper Cub. And so I had it to do all over again, but the Navy said there was two ways to fly, the right way and the Navy way. Whatever flight experience you had, they said they would knock that out of us so we could start over. Went through the War Training Service, WTS program, and I was sent to another school called "preflight," which, paradoxically, is after you learn how to fly. This was in Iowa City, Iowa, University of Iowa; and this was a fairly rigorous physical conditioning course. We had about four hours of calisthenics and sports and drill, close-order drill, a day; and you had four hours of academics. Upon leaving there in the spring of '44, I was sent to another flight school called "primary flight school," and that was Grosse Ile, Michigan. It was on an old Navy base that was on an island in the middle of the Detroit River, just south of Detroit. I served or trained there for some three months. And in the middle of '44 -- yeah, that's right. In the middle of '44, my class, most of my class, was eliminated from flight training because there, ostensively, were too many would-be Naval aviators in the pipeline, and they thought the war was coming to a close, and they wouldn't be needing as many Naval aviators. So I was -- I tried to get into the Navy electronics courses.

sp.speaker: Harold Phillips
sp.p: What was your grade when you had --

sp.speaker: Robert Noyer
sp.p: I was a cadet.

sp.speaker: Harold Phillips
sp.p: Basic cadet?

sp.speaker: Robert Noyer
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Harold Phillips
sp.p: And you held that grade all through your V-5 training?

sp.speaker: Robert Noyer
sp.p: Yes. You're an NavCad from the time you go in until the time you're commissioned. Then you're commissioned as an ensign.

sp.speaker: Harold Phillips
sp.p: And then when you were released from that program, what grade did you hold then?

sp.speaker: Robert Noyer
sp.p: Then I was reduced to a seaman, first class.

sp.speaker: Harold Phillips
sp.p: That's pretty good. You mentioned, part of your training consisted of all the calisthenics. Did you have the basic training that the Navy usually gives to boot camp?

sp.speaker: Robert Noyer
sp.p: Well, I suspect so. Ours was -- we had a lot of competition training. We had track and wrestling and boxing.

sp.speaker: Harold Phillips
sp.p: Did you get the weapons firing, that type of thing?

sp.speaker: Robert Noyer
sp.p: No, we didn't.

sp.speaker: Harold Phillips
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert Noyer
sp.p: We weren't firing weapons yet.

sp.speaker: Harold Phillips
sp.p: Okay. And so when you were released from the program, what happened next, then?

sp.speaker: Robert Noyer
sp.p: So I was sent to another school in Norman, Oklahoma. And this -- this course was for an aviation ordnanceman. I guess the present grade might be a ___, that type of thing.

sp.speaker: Harold Phillips
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert Noyer
sp.p: This -- we also had -- were given all the training on all types of weapons that would be on a Naval aircraft, the 30-caliber, the 50-caliber, 20-millimeter cannon, and bomb delivery systems. And we also had some gunnery training there, like skeet and trapshooting. I think that they probably thought some of us might be going into a rear-seat gunner or a belly-turret gunner. So we had that trap and skeet shooting, which was really -- I loved to do that. That was an expensive thing, but it didn't cost me a nickel. We also had some training as radar operators. And after -- after that, I was sent to a -- I was sent to a carrier air service unit called "CASU," like "cashew" nuts, C-A-S-U. And we were put together as a group, and we were there, again, training as a group to go aboard a new carrier, and the carrier was going to be the Coral Sea. It was a CVB-42, the whole number 42. This was a super carrier, the largest carrier in those days. So the entire ship's company was put together on the land -- on land to train, so when the carrier was launched, we could get aboard, go through shakedown, and we would have a trained crew. This was at a base outside of Atlantic City, New Jersey, a place called Pomona Naval Air Station. And now it's the home of the Atlantic City Municipal Airport. It has large runways and some big hangers. It still exists. I have flown in there with my own airplane many times. So after we got out of -- after CASU-26 was supposedly fully trained, we were all sent to Bayonne, New Jersey, where the ship, the Coral Sea, was still in the -- under construction. It was almost done, but we all went aboard and while the ship was kind of being done around us. The noise was -- it was impossible to sleep, because they were running rivet guns and chipping hammers and stuff all day and night. They were working three shifts on it. During the time I was on there, I was sent to Quonset Point, Rhode Island, for training on a new 20-millimeter aircraft gun called the "Cannon," I guess. I was sent up there for a month or so and then back to the ship. The ship was finally launched. But just prior to the ship's being launched, the President, Franklin D. Roosevelt died, and so they decided to change the name of the ship from the Coral Sea -- since it hadn't been launched yet, they changed it to "Franklin D. Roosevelt," otherwise known as "FDR CVB-42." It was then the largest carrier that had ever been built. And we went on a shakedown trip to Guantanamo Bay, GTMO Bay. The highlight of that was, we ran aground at GTMO Bay and were stuck there for a couple days. And the captain was -- his name was Soucek, he was one of two brothers. I forget which one he was. But after pumping out some of the fuel and getting all the tugs they could find, they hauled us off. And then in running aground, we bent a propeller shaft, which was almost impossible, in my mind, to do, since the propeller shafts were probably 18 to 20 inches in diameter, but -- So we left there, and we were to make a speed run to Rio. And the reason we were going to Rio was that they just elected -- democratically elected a new president of Brazil, and so they were to go down there and show the flag. So we went down at a high rate of speed, but the ship vibrated quite a bit. And I had a bunk that was stern, and the -- it was like dry dock all over again. It was really bad between the vibration and the noise. And during the trip down there, we had aircraft launch and retrieval on almost a continuous basis to get everybody up to speed. We put in down there, and I had the dubious distinction of being a cashier in a -- how shall I put this? -- in a house of less sterling repute. The reason for all of this was, these two destroyer escorts that were with us steamed in ahead of us by a day. And the sailors, at least half of them, got shore leave and were -- had gone to these various houses. And when the FDR came in, the same thing was happening, but they had raised the prices, causing a considerable disruption in the local economy. So to keep everything straight, the one section of the liberty section was sent with other SPs to these various houses, and we were to keep order and make change, I guess. That's -- that's kind of an odd thing. Not too many people have had that duty. We came back and went into dry dock and immediately -- to repair the damage and had to change out the shaft, I guess, in one of the huge screws or, in the parlance of the Navy, wheels, the propellers, so-called, had large chunks out of it where it run into the rocks. So we just had the usual shipboard duties of trying to keep busy. But they thought we were going to actually launch the carrier again after it was finished, and there would be -- it was still wartime. The war, I guess, was concluded in '45, April, I believe, the European war. And then in August of '45, the Japanese -- the Pacific war was concluded. So between that -- between those two times, we just kind of sat around and waited to collect points. It was a lot of make-work. We did overhauling of guns and cleaning of guns and building ammunition and a lot of make-work stuff.

sp.speaker: Harold Phillips
sp.p: Did you actually do some firing as a gunner off of a carrier?

sp.speaker: Robert Noyer
sp.p: Yes. I had a -- I had a couple of flights, and they were quite exciting, especially when someone else is doing the flying. You always feel kind of odd when you're sitting backwards, and someone else is doing to flying. When the war was over, or when I got out in April of '46, I had, I guess, enough points on April '46. I took my mustering-out pay and hitchhiked home, and I got home six weeks later. The distance was about 500 miles, but I come -- had a real good time going home. When I got home, I applied for a program called the "52-20 Club." That's where you, if you -- they can't give you a job, you could get $20 a week for 52 weeks. Unfortunately, on my separation papers, I had put down that I had previously been a welder. I was out of work about three days after I got home. I had to go back to work as a -- So I went -- I worked until about June or July, I think, and I went down to Purdue and applied for admission, and I had a transfer of credits of a year from before the war at Ball State Teachers College. I had taken calculus, D-calculus, I should say; chemistry; physics; and drafting, mechanical drafting. So when I got to Purdue, I didn't have to take any freshman courses, and I was admitted with that standing and chopped a year off of my -- what would have been four years.

sp.speaker: Harold Phillips
sp.p: Did you use the GI bill?

sp.speaker: Robert Noyer
sp.p: Yes, I used the GI bill with a great deal of relish. Previously, I wanted to be a doctor, before the war, but I don't think my father had the money for it, and I didn't think I could work my way through medical school and still pass through. And I had always been interested in electronics, and I had been an amateur experimenter before the war, so I went into electrical engineering. And I used the GI bill and graduated from '49 -- in '49 from Purdue.

sp.speaker: Harold Phillips
sp.p: What grade were you when you left the Navy?

sp.speaker: Robert Noyer
sp.p: AOU, aviation ordnanceman utility, I guess -- it used to be AOM, aviation -- well, I don't know what it was, AOM something, anyhow -- AOU. So I am glad I was out of there. I didn't learn anything that was worth anything to speak of except for the flying. And after that was over, it wasn't worth much. I had very few significant experiences except that I didn't get hurt.

sp.speaker: Harold Phillips
sp.p: Yeah. Didn't crash.

sp.speaker: Robert Noyer
sp.p: I didn't crash. I didn't burn. I did do a foolish thing once on a carrier. We were having flight operations, and I'm standing on the catwalk that's about four feet below the deck, the flight deck, watching night operations, and that was a duty station. And an airplane came back with a five-inch rocket still attached to the wing mounts. And when he hit his hook, his tail hook didn't work, so he -- they erected this barrier, which is a series of fence made out of one-and-a-half inch cables with hydraulic reels that let the cable out so that when it catches the front of the airplane, it doesn't stop it immediately. It's like the hooks -- like, cables that tail hook catches on, but these are elevated in the front of the airplanes. So when the airplane came to a rapid halt, the five-inch rocket left the rocket launching rail under the wing and fell onto the deck and slithered along the deck, and it was arming itself. The arming wire had been left armed in the aircraft, and when it left the aircraft, there is a little propeller in the nose. And to keep the propeller from going around, there's a wire that goes through that, back up to the bomb rack. So if you want to drop the rocket, dispose of it without arming it, you don't arm it in the cockpit. You make sure that the wire stays with it. Unfortunately, the thing, in some way, became armed. So it slithered along the deck and stopped almost in front of me with the little propeller turning. After the propeller turns an equivalent of 150 feet of air, it's fully armed, and if you touch the nose of it or bang it, why, it will go off, and it was made out of the five-inch shell. The nickname for the rocket was called "Holy Moses," I guess, because when the first one went off, the guy said, "Holy Moses." So I had had training on the -- on this rocket and on the fuse. So I just scrambled up on the flight deck and picked it up -- they weigh about 60 pounds -- and dropped it over the side. I must say that I was extremely lucky, because along the sides of the carrier, down almost at water level, there are gun tubs sticking out that had quad 40s in them, that are served by three or four Marines. And the saying is, I had my chance; I could have knocked off three or four Marines. But fortunately, I didn't drop it into the gun tub. I dumped it in the sea, and as soon as it hit the water, it went off with a large explosion. And I was called up to the executive officers' quarters and given considerable advice at that point. And I was lucky I wasn't court-martialed or given a captain's mast or something. But I thought I was doing right at the time.

sp.speaker: Harold Phillips
sp.p: A heroic action, yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert Noyer
sp.p: I might have -- I might have killed four or five people, or I might have gotten hurt myself. And that was --

sp.speaker: Harold Phillips
sp.p: You certainly should have gotten a citation for it, though.

sp.speaker: Robert Noyer
sp.p: I was -- I think if I had said two words to the exec, I would have gotten a citation, like -- like 30 days on ___. That's -- that's about the majority of my service. I -- What was it like coming home? Well, it was great. There were no parades, and we just came dribbling home and went to work. And I was kind of amazed at the -- to be a civilian again. I only had to get up when my mother made me, and I had to go to work when my boss wanted me to.

sp.speaker: Harold Phillips
sp.p: You mentioned that you flew in and out of the airport in New Jersey. When did you get your pilot's license?

sp.speaker: Robert Noyer
sp.p: I got my pilot's license right after the war, went back to Purdue. I had all the requirements for it, but I had no reason to get one. And during the war, almost all civil aviation was shut down, except for some civil air patrol type of thing. So as soon as I got out, I got my ticket. And later on, several years later, I was able to buy an airplane. And I have had -- I have been flying -- I soloed in '41. I got my ticket in '46 when I got out, and I have been flying ever since.

sp.speaker: Harold Phillips
sp.p: Did you stay active in the reserves at all?

sp.speaker: Robert Noyer
sp.p: Well, there's another story. If nothing else, it's funny. I was working in Long Island, developing our present color TV system, and I was only making $66 a week. And I had a wife and two children. So I thought, why not go back in the reserves and get a little money? It's easy money. So in June of 1950, I went to Floyd Bennett ___, and the next week, the Korean War started. By October, I had received orders to report to Task Force 77 in California for duty on a carrier to go to Korea. I was not very happy about this. And we had a draft -- or a military coordinator at the company I worked for, and he had me transferred to a secret project, secret military project, at which point I got my orders rescinded, and I didn't have to go to Korea. And we now step ahead to June of 1951 -- no. Excuse me -- to September of 1951, and we find me in Korea as a civilian. So I guess I was -- shot myself in both feet. I was sent to Korea with a -- I was a team leader for a team of six other engineers, and we were to install and evaluate prototype equipment that will tell the radio operator who is a friend and who is a foe. The equipment is called "IFF." It's the job I was on before I was sent to Korea. I was on a design team to convert wartime Mark-5 IFF to Mark-10 IFF. So I took 12 -- 12 kits, prototype kits, to Korea to put on the search radars, because we were having difficulty in determining who was -- who was a good fellow and who was a bad fellow. So I ended up in Korea after all.

sp.speaker: Harold Phillips
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert Noyer
sp.p: During this time, Christmas came, and my wife is by herself, and she has the two children -- and I think it was Christmas -- the day of Christmas Eve, the 24th -- had a knock on the door. And an enlisted man was there inquiring as to my whereabouts, saying that I hadn't been to drill for three or four weekends, something like that, three or four months. He wanted to know why and all that. And my wife is a very mild-mannered person, but she needed to fill him in. The proof of the story is, when I came back from Korea, I went up to the Naval air station to see the commanding officer of the reserve that I was affiliated or connected with. And he inquired of the -- of his orderly whether my wife was with me, and he said, "No." So he ushered me in and gave me a big handshake and told me what a good thing I was doing, and he said that he had conversation with my wife, because my wife had called him up Christmas Eve, I think, or Christmas Day, and gave him some information. So we're back to flying.

sp.speaker: Harold Phillips
sp.p: Is that the end of your military experience, then?

sp.speaker: Robert Noyer
sp.p: Yes, it is. However, after that I worked with the military as a civilian engineer for some, probably, 10 or 12 years more in various capacities. I had an office in Weisbaden. I was a European operations manager for an electronics company that built IFF, and the equivalent, to modify radars, and I worked with several other companies. I went from the company that I was originally with, with several other companies, and still in the electronics business and mostly with the military. So, in effect, I guess I have been with the military for a long time, at least in some capacity.

sp.speaker: Harold Phillips
sp.p: Did you ever go to any reunions of the FDR?

sp.speaker: Robert Noyer
sp.p: We never had any reunions. I never knew about it. I saw in the newspaper quite a few years ago that the FDR was in the yards in Kearny, New Jersey, which is K-E-A-R-N-Y, and -- which is kind of odd because I was born in the other Kearney, that it was -- had been broken up. And I was only living in Pennsylvania then. I would have been glad to have gone up there and gotten a piece of it. I have a plank owner certificate from the FDR that was given to me by Mrs. Roosevelt, not -- I wasn't the only one. She passed them out to all the crew that were on it when she was -- when the FDR was commissioned.

sp.speaker: Harold Phillips
sp.p: So your final grade was first class when you were released?

sp.speaker: Robert Noyer
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Harold Phillips
sp.p: Ordnance?

sp.speaker: Robert Noyer
sp.p: Yes. The -- well, I would say we talked about what was of any use to me. The military is always of use to you, unless it kills you. I think I learned some more discipline. I was not undisciplined at the time, but I learned to be very punctual. This occurred notwithstanding, but I did learn punctuality, and I learned respect for rate and rank, and I think it improved my study habits, because a great deal of my time seemed to have been spent in academics of one kind of another.

sp.speaker: Harold Phillips
sp.p: Do you mind commenting on how you got involved with the B-17?

sp.speaker: Robert Noyer
sp.p: Yes. No, I wouldn't mind.

sp.speaker: Harold Phillips
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Robert Noyer
sp.p: I wear a jacket that has a nice, embroidered depiction of a B-17G on the back. And in England the B-17 is the "Aluminum Overcast," and that's for obvious reasons. It's so big that when flying over, it looks like an aluminum overcast. People ask me about that, and I have to explain it to them. It's owned by the Experimental Aircraft Association in Oshkosh, Wisconsin. They have quite a few airplanes in the museum, but they maintain the B-17 as a -- kind of a flying museum. It flies around the country, in the north in the summertime, and the south in the wintertime. You pay a fairly large sum for a half-hour ride, most of it going as a charitable -- not a deduction, but it goes to charity, to keep the thing going. It's a very expensive airplane to operate. And they also give you a jacket. So that's how I got the jacket. And I like the jacket, anyhow, and it makes friends. I made a lot of B-17 friends. I have to tell them that I'm kind of a counterfeit. I think they all understand that.

sp.speaker: Harold Phillips
sp.p: Were you involved in its appearance here at Winchester during the Apple Blossom?

sp.speaker: Robert Noyer
sp.p: No. Well, I was -- I bought a ride on it, and I wrote a "Slice of Life" -- I used to write a "Slice of Life" column for the Winchester Star, until they decided that the authors weren't any good, and they quit it. I said, "Thanks a lot." And I wrote some more, over a hundred of them. But having -- having to do with it, I support the EAA, and I talk with the guys in there and ran a few errands for them, and I wrote the "Slice of Life" about that, and it was published in the paper then, and I gave the crew copies of it, and they liked it. It was somewhat -- it was a mildly -- {coughs} excuse me -- it was a mildly sentimental piece. I usually write just straight humor. I'm not too good on -- on jerking up the tears.

sp.speaker: Harold Phillips
sp.p: Did you join the VFW, American Legion, or anything of those?

sp.speaker: Robert Noyer
sp.p: No, no. I was a bartender in the American Legion in Lafayette, Indiana, because I needed money.

sp.speaker: Harold Phillips
sp.p: Yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert Noyer
sp.p: And I never joined either of the two organizations.

sp.speaker: Harold Phillips
sp.p: Did you ever receive any special citations or awards?

sp.speaker: Robert Noyer
sp.p: No, no. In fact, they were probably pretty glad to get rid of me. I was a drain on the -- on the public trough.

sp.speaker: Harold Phillips
sp.p: I would doubt that. Is there anything else that you would like to add?

sp.speaker: Robert Noyer
sp.p: Well, I think this -- the program that you're a part of is a good thing. I know from one role of genealogical work that I have done, that if you don't talk to some of the old people, it's going to all be gone. I've erred in that area. My mother and father are both gone now, but my mother was big on this genealogy. And my son, Dr. Rolf, R-O-L-F, has done a lot of work in genealogy. He's gone way back to 15-, 1600s in Europe. He's an excellent researcher. So he's doing that, and I think it's -- if we don't do this, it's all going to be lost.

sp.speaker: Harold Phillips
sp.p: How did you get to Winchester? I forgot to ask that.

sp.speaker: Robert Noyer
sp.p: Well, it's like, how do you get to Carnegie Hall? I was -- I wanted to -- I wanted to retire, because I was really tired of working overseas, mostly. And my wife lost the sight in one eye, and the other eye was not good, and she could no longer drive. And I was spending a lot of time overseas for the company I was working for. So I -- I couldn't, very well, retire where I lived. I used to live in Vienna, Virginia, about 75 miles east of here, but the cost of living and the -- and the general hubbub was more than I could cope with. So we wanted a place that we could put my airplane that we both use to go around the county to see our friends and relatives, and we also wanted a good library. So we found this library and the big airport, and we are happy as larks. We still use the library, and I have a very small airplane now that I keep out at the airport. We're very happy to be in Winchester, very happy with the people and facilities and just the general tenor of the place.

sp.speaker: Harold Phillips
sp.p: Well, thank you very much. It's been very interesting.

sp.speaker: Robert Noyer
sp.p: It's my pleasure. And thank you for asking me. (End of interview.)
